summary:
West Java stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Sub-national variation sits inside that framework. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. West Java carries no equivalent religious-law regime, but its police act against LGBT gatherings regardless of whether an offence has occurred.

On 22 June 2025 the West Java Regional Police detained 75 people, 74 men and one woman, at a privately rented villa in the Puncak area of Bogor Regency after a tip from local residents. Police described the event as an LGBT "family gathering" held to avoid detection. Amnesty International reported the arrests on 24 June 2025, called the operation a discriminatory raid and a blatant violation of human rights and privacy, stated that the gathering violated no law, and demanded release and accountability. Tempo reported the arrests on 25–26 June 2025.

Street violence against trans women in West Java is documented and, so far, unprosecuted. Pelangi Nusantara recorded ten attacks on 45 victim-survivors in Bogor between 30 March and 15 July 2026, in which groups of 10–20 men punched, kicked and hurled stones, glass bottles and firecrackers at trans women, stripped some of them naked and filmed the assaults for social media under the account @bogorbersihlgbt ("Bogor clean of LGBT"). No alleged perpetrator has been publicly identified, arrested or prosecuted. A trans-rights activist who accompanied women filing police reports said officers accepted the case but worked on it half-heartedly, and some survivors were too afraid to report. ABC News reported on 15 August 2026 an attack in which men doused a trans woman with what looked like urine on a street in Bogor, one of a wave of attacks; a trans woman quoted in that report said those who previously appeared in public now live in fear.

Activists link the violence to a presidential regulation issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 that lists nonmilitary threats and classifies the "spread of LGBTQ culture" as a risk to be monitored and controlled within national defence policy, and to discriminatory regional regulations. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to the wave of vigilante attacks, with commentators quoted by ABC News stating that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy and that state language legitimises violence against trans women.

Trans travellers have died in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.
tangentialFactors:
West Java differs from the provinces with the sharpest statutory exposure. Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise same-sex sexual activity directly, and Aceh's caning sentences are imposed under provincial religious law; West Java's exposure runs through national morality provisions, police discretion and regional regulations rather than a local religious code.

The Puncak villa operation shows the gap between legality and enforcement. Amnesty International's finding that the gathering violated no law did not prevent 75 detentions, which means an event carrying no criminal liability can still produce arrest, detention and public exposure for attendees, including foreign visitors present at the time.

Enforcement in West Java is triggered by community reporting. The villa raid followed a tip from local residents, and the attacks on trans women were filmed and circulated by an account presenting itself as a neighbourhood clean-up campaign, indicating that hostility operates through both official channels and informal mobilisation.

National policy language and local violence are treated by researchers as connected. Activists quoted across the 2025 and 2026 reporting argue that the presidential regulation and discriminatory regional regulations gave official cover to street attacks, a causal claim made by the activists and commentators rather than established by any court or inquiry.

The custody death of Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla is recorded at national level and is not specific to West Java, but it is the only documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody and bears on how any visitor, in any province, may be treated after arrest.
localsOnly:
Indonesians cannot enter a same-sex marriage, so the extra-marital sex provision of the 2026 penal code applies to same-sex couples without a route to exemption through marriage.

Trans women in Bogor have altered their daily conduct since the 2026 attacks. Those quoted by ABC News said they no longer appear in public as they previously did and live in fear of being identified on the street.

Reporting to police is a documented obstacle for local survivors. Some of the 45 victim-survivors were too afraid to file complaints, and an activist who accompanied women who did file said officers took the cases on but worked on them half-heartedly. No alleged perpetrator has been publicly identified, arrested or prosecuted in connection with the ten attacks.

Regional regulations in force in West Java are cited by activists as discriminatory toward LGBT people, alongside the October 2025 presidential regulation that places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled.

Residents who organise or attend private LGBT gatherings face police attention on the basis of neighbour reports, as occurred at the Puncak villa on 22 June 2025, even where the gathering itself breaks no law.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not state whether any of the 75 people detained at the Puncak villa were subsequently charged, tried or released, or on what basis any charge would have rested given Amnesty International's finding that no law was broken.

Unresolved: no source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition in Indonesia, whether a trans visitor's gender marker on an Indonesian or foreign passport will be accepted at Indonesian entry points, or how airport screening treats documents that do not match a traveller's presentation.

Unresolved: whether the extra-marital sex provision of the penal code that took effect on 2 January 2026 has been used in any prosecution in West Java is not sourced here; the available reporting describes national prosecutions as selective rather than systematic.

Unresolved: no source records whether the attacks on trans women in Bogor were investigated as hate crimes or whether any sentencing enhancement for bias-motivated violence exists under Indonesian or West Javanese law.

Unresolved: access to gender-affirming healthcare, hormone medication and competent HIV care for visitors in West Java is not covered by this inventory, and no facility-level information is available.

Unresolved: the competing accounts of Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla's death, his mother's allegation of police beatings and the police denial of violence, have not been reconciled in the sources cited here.
